The complete theory of Empty is not docs#FirstOrder.Language.Theory.IsSatisfiable:

import Mathlib

instance : FirstOrder.Language.empty.Structure Empty where

theorem empty_theory_not_satisfiable :
    ¬(FirstOrder.Language.empty.completeTheory Empty).IsSatisfiable := by
  intro ⟨model⟩ -- satisfiable means exists a nonempty model
  let emptySentence : FirstOrder.Language.empty.Sentence :=
    .all .falsum -- `∀ x, False`
  have mem : emptySentence ∈ FirstOrder.Language.empty.completeTheory Empty :=
    isEmptyElim -- `Empty` verifies `∀ x, False`
  apply model.nonempty'.elim -- model is nonempty
  exact model.is_model.realize_of_mem emptySentence mem

This seems like a mistake to me. Surely we want the theories coming from a model structure to always be satisfiable?
yes, but i believe models are supposed to be non-empty by definition?
so this structure is not a model?
Surealy we want every structure to be a model of its own theory?
we want every model to be a model of it's own theory... not so sure about structure though...
Well you can't talk about models without having already fixed a theory
yes? and?
(i could be wrong though, i'm checking my model theory textbook)

here's a quote from Sets, Models and Proofs by Ieke Moerdijk and Jaap van Oosten:

Remark 2.3.4
In modern textbooks on model theory one seldom finds the requirement that the underlying set of an LLL-structure must be nonempty, and certainly there are good reasons to allow the empty set as an LLL-structure (provided LLL has no constants): consider the definition of a substructure generated by a subset [...] and the proof of [the downward Löwenheim-Skolem Theorem], where the nonemptiness requirement is quite inelegant. Nevertheless, we stick to the old-fashioned convention that structures must be nonempty because it is harder to formulate a sound and complete proof system for possibly empty structures. Indeed, the empty structure satisfies ∀xφ\forall x\varphi∀xφ, for any formula ϕ\phiϕ.
so apparently it is a matter of convention.
in mathlib structures (docs#FirstOrder.Language.Structure) don't have to be nonempty
but (nonempty) models (docs#FirstOrder.Language.Theory.ModelType) do
right, so if you want your statement to be true (every structure is a model for its theory) we should either make models not require nonemptiness, or make structures require it.

I was thinking the solution would be to change the definition of "satisfiable" from "there exists a nonempty model of the theory" to "there exists a structure satisfying the theory", the only difference from the current definition would be the structure is allowed to be empty
i suspect that the nonemptiness requirement is there for good reason, even if i don't know it.
perhaps another person who knows the subject can comment on this?
the motivation is to remove some spurious Nonempty assumptions I found
apparently, the're not so spurious

I am not a model theorist, but I always thought that the existence of a model actually implies that the theory is consistent. If everything has an empty model, then this could be problematic.

I view it as "you could in theory make the choice that the empty set is connected" (but you would be wrong).

Damiano Testa said:

If everything has an empty model, then this could be problematic.

Of course not everything has an empty model. If you have any constant symbols at all then they won't have an interpretation in the empty set. And if your theory contains docs#FirstOrder.Language.nonemptyTheory then obviously the empty set won't be a model.

so after asking [LLM], i think i've discovered a decent point: The statement T⊨φT\models \varphiT⊨φ becomes false when TTT has an empty model and φ\varphiφ is an existential, as the semantics of T⊨φT\models \varphiT⊨φ is "for every model M\mathcal{M}M of TTT, M⊨φ\mathcal{M}\models \varphiM⊨φ"...
another point it made is that you can make this change, but you should then not use standard first-order logic, but instead something called "free logic"
if T can't guarantee that anything exists then it doesn't guarantee that anything exists
that makes sense

elaborating on that first point, you get that the following general rules of deduction are false:

  • ∀x,P(X)→∃x,P(x)\forall x, P(X) \rightarrow \exists x, P(x)∀x,P(X)→∃x,P(x)
  • ∀x,φ(x)⊢φ(y)\forall x, \varphi(x) \vdash \varphi(y)∀x,φ(x)⊢φ(y)
  • ∃x,x=x\exists x, x = x∃x,x=x
well yeah those are all false in the empty model, they are true in every other model
and you can't prove those in Lean without adding a Nonempty assumption
exactly, but in particular that second one sometimes comes baked in as a rule of deduction in FOL
i do agree that it seems kind of spurious though
that sound weird, then I can prove things like ∃x,x=x\exists x, x = x∃x,x=x (because I can prove ∀y,∃x,x=x\forall y, \exists x, x = x∀y,∃x,x=x)
yes, exactly
the "weird" aspect of this logic (imo) is that φ(x)⊢∃y,φ(y)\varphi(x) \vdash \exists y, \varphi(y)φ(x)⊢∃y,φ(y) is not valid.
what? why not?
isn't that just Exists.intro
but you've proven that there is something in the domain of discourse?
if ϕ(x):=x=x\phi(x) := x = xϕ(x):=x=x, then this is clearly false, no?
since x=xx=xx=x is provable?
yeah x=xx = xx=x is provable
but if you have an xxx then you have an xxx
that's a thing in your domain of discourse
no, that's just a variable
it doesn't need to be a thing in your domain of discourse
then you should've bound it with a ∀\forall∀ quantifier
we can't be having unbound variables here
idk what to tell you, you can have unbound variables in logic, it's common.
or you should've added it to the context
there is no such thing in FOL i believe?
surely you have to keep track of the free variables you have?
yes: you see those in the formulas.
when they're not there, they're gone.
this lets you prove bogus theorems such as ∀x,ϕ(x)⊢∃x,ϕ(x)\forall x, \phi(x) \vdash \exists x, \phi(x)∀x,ϕ(x)⊢∃x,ϕ(x)
because you can open a free variable without closing it
idk what to tell you, that's just FOL
well we don't even have FOL in mathlib
anyway, you might feel enlightened/enpassioned when you read the wikipedia page for free logic.

Edward van de Meent said:

anyway, you might feel enlightened/enpassioned when you read the wikipedia page for free logic.

after reading the wikipedia page, free logic also seems a bit weird: there can be terms that don't denote any object

i have little experience with the semantics of free logic, but i was once in the situation where i wanted to prove that one can relativize theorems to (nonempty) classes by relativizing every proof step.
For a free logic variant of natural deduction there would have been a simple and beautiful syntactic transformation for every proof rule, but for standard natural deduction this approach was breaking down, precisely because of the existence of these "bad proofs" like
(∀x,ϕ(x))⊢(∃x,ϕ(x))(\forall x, \phi(x)) \vdash (\exists x,\phi(x))(∀x,ϕ(x))⊢(∃x,ϕ(x))
which intrinsically use the built-in nonemptyness of standard fol
i believe there the solution (not involving free logic) was basically to invoke the gödel completeness theorem and prove the wanted result from a semantic point of view (using ⊨\vDash⊨)
all things i didn't want to introduce at that point

It's not a bogus theorem in the context of the intended semantics. This is true in any non-empty structure.

Yes, historically FOL has not typically been formalized with a notion of contexts.

The question of the empty model is indeed a divisive one. I think most of the model theory community just exclude the empty model from everything, but @Antoine Chambert-Loir and I disagree quite strongly with this convention. And yes, it means that you have to formalize FOL with contexts, but I claim this is the morally correct way to do anyways.

That said, this is certainly a nonstandard opinion, so I can understand that Mathlib decided to follow the standard conventions.
I could also see this as just being an oversight, since "satisfiable" is defined as "the ModelType of the theory is nonempty" and a ModelType is a bundled nonempty structure satisfying the theory

I believe the contexts Anatole is referring to pop up when defining the syntactical notion of derivation.
On the semantic side it indeed is (I believe) just the question of using nonempty structures vs all structures.

But since one will typically eventually be interested in both, this choice has a real impact and is not an oversight
related, a theory modeling a formula also does not consider the empty model

I'm intrigued by this, are you saying that one can't give a working Hilbert Style deduction system for inclusive fol? (Since Gentzen and Fitch-style systems would probably count as having a context/variable tracking?)
that sounds like it should be possible too

related, a theory modeling a formula also does not consider the empty model

This is typically called entailment of a formula, and T⊨ϕT \vDash \phiT⊨ϕ is supposed to be equivalent to
unsat(T∪¬ϕ)\text{unsat}(T \cup {\neg\phi})unsat(T∪¬ϕ) which i think requires the definitions to use the same notion of model
maybe we should just drop the requirement that a docs#FirstOrder.Language.Theory.ModelType be nonempty?

The standard Hilbert style deduction don't allow empty structures because of the implicit universal quantification and, in the end ∀x,P(x)⇒∃x,P(x)\forall x, P(x) \Rightarrow \exists x, P(x)∀x,P(x)⇒∃x,P(x) is a “theorem”. Several logicians advocated for deduction rules that prevent this, starting with Quine. Sequent calculus, where the context can hold variables, is a good way to do so.
you would just have to always have explicit universal quantifiers

Try to do that for 5 minutes and see how painful it is.

When we start a sentence with “Let GGG be a group and let g,hg, hg,h be elements of GGG such that gh=hgg h = h ggh=hg, then…”, we actually add an object GGG to the context together with two elements of GGG and the hypothesis that the commute. And the rest of the proof uses that without quantifying everything.

In particular, the negation of a given sentence (say g−1h=hg−1g^{-1} h = h g^{-1}g−1h=hg−1) still keeps G,g,hG, g, hG,g,h in the context, and doesn't negate the implied universal quantifier.
even with just predicate calculus I've found it difficult to work with the hilbert style deduction system

Anatole Dedecker said:

The question of the empty model is indeed a divisive one. I think most of the model theory community just exclude the empty model from everything, but @Antoine Chambert-Loir and I disagree quite strongly with this convention. And yes, it means that you have to formalize FOL with contexts, but I claim this is the morally correct way to do anyways.

Allowing empty structures breaks prenex normal form, which is something model theorists use pretty frequently.
Even though I am somewhat sympathetic to the idea, I would still argue that the 'moral' advantage of allowing empty structures is outweighed by this in practice.
Ah, this is a very good point, the first really convincing for me. Thanks !

It is very easy to find statements that depend on set XXX and that only hold provided XXX is nonempty. This does not make the empty set inexistent. It means that you should assume XXX is nonempty when you state your theorem.
To be clear, I find arguing that there is no empty structure as misguided as arguing that there is no empty type (or set)
Ok, but do you feel the same about empty models?
Perhaps the point is that "X models phi" should only be defined when phi has no free variables?
if you like nonempty models so much we could introduce a new typeclass for theories whose models are all nonempty

Edward van de Meent said:

Ok, but do you feel the same about empty models?

Yes. More precisely, what I expect is that FOL is sound with respect to all structures. Including the empty one. I.e. if you have a proof of ϕ\phiϕ from some collection of premises, and you have a structure that validates all premises, then it also validates ϕ\phiϕ. This also works if you have no premises, in which case every structure (including the empty one) validates ϕ\phiϕ.

Edward van de Meent said:

Perhaps the point is that "X models phi" should only be defined when phi has no free variables?

If ϕ\phiϕ has free variables, and you want to interpret it in some structure, then you have to first choose an assignment of values for the free variables in your structure. For example x1=x2x_1 = x_2x1​=x2​ can be true or false in N\mathbb NN depending on how I interpret x1x_1x1​ and x2x_2x2​. It is not universally true of course.

I agree with all of these sentiments, but James provided an example of a fundamental result of of FOL/model theory which breaks non trivially if you allow empty models. This raises some issues about how far the theory could be pushed. This at least justifies why model theorists usually disregard empty models.

But you don't need to disregard the empty model in order to state this result. The result is: given a formula, there is another formula with all quantifiers in front, such that the two are equivalent modulo the assumption ∃x\exists x∃x
Disregarding the empty model is letting the tail wag the dog. The tail is logic, the dog semantics.

So you're saying that because tons of important theorems about filters assume NeBot, to the extent that mathlib made docs#Filter.NeBot a class, we should have instead assumed that Bot was not a filter? (of course I know you're not saying this at all :-) )

I think that one way of reconciling James + Anatole's sentiments is allowing empty structures but creating an analogous class to carry around the nonemptiness assumption.

This would however have a serious drawback in that it looks like it would force us to diverge from the literature. We did diverge from the literature when it came to filters. But filters are not so commonly used whereas model theory is an entire area of mathematics, so breaking conventions is a lot more dangerous -- it is far more likely to lead to confusion.

looking through the definition of prenex normal form, it looks like the only thing to look out for is making sure that you don't accidentally bind free variables? or am i missing something?
e.g. for (∃xϕ)∧φ(\exists x \phi) \wedge \varphi(∃xϕ)∧φ, you don't normalize to ∃x(ϕ∧φ)\exists x (\phi \wedge \varphi)∃x(ϕ∧φ) but instead to ∃x′(ϕ[x′/x]∧φ\exists x' (\phi[x'/x] \wedge \varphi∃x′(ϕ[x′/x]∧φ where x′x'x′ is not used in φ\varphiφ.

Aaron Liu said:

if your prenex normal forms don't work for empty models you can just assume they're nonempty separately, without baking it into the definition of a model

Focusing on the empty model is kind of misleading here I think. The question is, do we want our proof system to prove ∃x,⊤\exists x, \top∃x,⊤ ? If yes, then we lose soundness for empty models. If not, then prenex normal form breaks.

Alternatively we could say that the proof system for nonempty models is the general proof system but with one extra variable always in context. This would work, but is probably a bit of painful duplication.

This is also why the situation is worse than for filters : if we choose to allow the empty models, it puts restrictions on our proof system, which will apply even to people who don't care about the empty model (e.g because they care about prenex normal form).
The "proof system for nonempty models" is simply FOL with the axiom ∃x,⊤\exists x,\top∃x,⊤

Well, depending on who you ask, FOL has this axiome essentially "baked in". In the usual presentation of natural deduction (which is, on equal footing with sequent calculus, the only valid proof system imho), this comes from the rule of introduction of the existencial quantifier, which puts no restrictions on what the witnessing term may depend on.

If you want a proof system that works for empty models, you need to work for it by keeping in your context a list of "valid variables", and the terms used to witness an existencial may only have free variables among those "valid variables"

For example, the Wikipedia page for "first order logic" lists as provable formulas things like (∀x,G)∧F  ⟺  ∀x,(G∧F)(\forall x, G) \land F \iff \forall x, (G \land F)(∀x,G)∧F⟺∀x,(G∧F). I disagree with this choice, but this is what people usually have in mind when they hear "first order logic"
I am well aware. My point is that there is no "painful duplication" if you define FOL correctly from the beginning.

Morally I agree, but in Lean I think without duplication the API may be quite painful. Not being able to put things in prenex form without thinking feels like a significant usability issue. Again, I agree with your opinion, I'm just saying that James gave us a good reason to follow the established convention.

This is not an established convention, as the quote from Moerdijk--van Oosten above made clear. I'd be surprised if you could find any categorically-minded logician who willingly uses this convention.

I am well aware of this (and again, I agree with you !). I'm just saying that we need to think of a way to allow model theorists to "just put things in prenex normal form" without thinking, and this may require creating an interface just for their wrong proof system (or maybe not, but either way we can't just ignore this !)
It'd be nice if someone could find a source where models aren't assumed to be nonempty

Edward van de Meent said:

It'd be nice if someone could find a source where models aren't assumed to be nonempty

Hodges allows structures to be empty. (Also, I allowed (metric) structures to be empty in my thesis, although honestly I'm not sure I accounted for all of the ramifications of that.)
In any case empty structures are also common in the context of Fraïssé limits, because they make the joint embedding property a special case of the amalgamation property.

In the end I feel like this is one of those situations where there's legitimately arguments for both conventions, similar to how sometimes it makes sense to require rings to have units and sometimes it doesn't.

I just find it pretty deeply annoying when people outside my field insist that there's no legitimate reason why this might be a common convention (and do things like refer to the consequences of this convention as 'bogus' or 'wrong').

Two remarks: 1) Hodges, and other books of his kind, are books on model theory, while this discussion pertains to proof theory.
2) The hierarchical structure is applied in theories whose models are obviously nonempty (integers, the Cantor set, etc.).

Antoine Chambert-Loir said:

while this discussion pertains to proof theory.

I thought this was about model theory? The top level folder in mathlib is ModelTheory/ and the type in question is docs#FirstOrder.Language.Theory.ModelType. How did proof theory get into this?

Semantic entailment ⊨\vDash⊨ and syntactic derivability ⊢\vdash⊢ are supposed to be equivalent via the gödel completeness theorem. So whatever choice you pick on one side, it will affect the other side
I.e. if you choose that models are nonempty on the semantics side, you need other syntactic proof systems

Or if you say "this proof system defines derivability in fol" and you proof system can/can't derive ∃x,x=x\exists x, x = x∃x,x=x from nothing, then you need to make your semantic definitions fit (if you want gödel completeness, and you do want that)
afaik Mathlib currently doesn't have any syntactic notions of derivability
But e.g. Floris and Han have defined something (in Lean 3, maybe it is not ported to lean 4 though) for their proof of the Independence of the continuum hypothesis
Btw: our current definition of formulae is adapted from that project!

Anatole Dedecker said:

Not being able to put things in prenex form without thinking feels like a significant usability issue.

What's wrong with just adding a typeclass assumption that your theory is nonempty?

If I may
1) The "theory of the empty structure" is an isolated point in the space of theories. So you can decide to remove it easily if you need to (for example if you need prenex forms)
2) For quantifier elimination, you really want empty substructures, otherwise statements are not equivalent to quantifier free statements. I personally believe the right definition of QE is that any formula phi(x) is equivalent to a formule psi(x) without quantifiers (with the same free variables). This is only equivalent to substructure completeness if you allow empty substructures.
3) As pointed out earlier there is an easy fix for proof theory with the empty structure (contexts!)
